The system garnered renewed interest after U −10 wt.% Mo was recognized as a viable option for monolithic LEU-based metal fuel foils (Hofman and Meyer 2002) for several research reactors within the USA. Molybdenum is a gamma-phase (body centered cubic, BCC) stabilizer in uranium which promotes a large solid solubility region with a peritectic reaction at higher Mo concentration. The region of greatest interest here is defined from pure uranium (0 wt.% Mo, 1408 K) to the liquid composition of the peritectic reaction (∼13.5 wt.% Mo, ∼1575 K). Cooling from the BCC solid solution, other phases are encountered through a peritectoid and eutectoid reaction involving the tetragonal and orthorhombic uranium allotropes as well as the U2Mo intermetallic.2 The scope here is limited to the (U,Mo) ←→(U,Mo) solidification reaction. This was high quality data especially considering it was some of the first experimentation on the system, ensuring the authors encountered many new challenges when working with uranium. It is an important observation that through 75 years and at least 10 relevant proposed phase diagrams, there has been a dearth of data relating to the uranium-rich solid/liquid phase region, leading to a relatively unconstrained phase boundary problem.
